🐊 ALLIGATORS – Beyond Earth, Beyond Limits.

Biz sadece Mars'ı haritalamıyoruz; geleceğin keşiflerine yön veriyoruz. Bilim, teknoloji ve takım ruhuyla sınırları aşmaya hazırız. Beş kişi, tek hedef: Mars'ın bilinmeyenlerini keşfetmek!

DREAM • BUILD • EXPLORE
summary:
MarsPath is an interactive 3D route-planning and survival-decision prototype for astronaut surface walks on Mars. Users choose start and destination points within two NASA-inspired sectors: Gale Crater with Mount Sharp, and Jezero Crater with the Neretva delta. Named landmarks such as Bradbury Landing open information cards on geology and elevation.

The challenge is that the shortest path can be lethal. Steep slopes, loose dune traps, sharp rock, extreme cold, radiation and gaps in radio coverage threaten astronauts, while oxygen and battery reserves are finite. MarsPath’s A* pathfinder computes three alternatives (safest, fastest and science-oriented) and scores each for these hazards and for estimated oxygen and battery use under a one-third oxygen rule, which preserves a return margin. It recommends one route, explains why, and suggests an EVA start hour from an hourly dust-storm scenario.

Why it matters: mission planners need tools that weigh safety, endurance and science before astronauts leave the lander. Making these trade-offs visible helps crews avoid dangerous routes yet still reach valuable science sites. Users can also upload real NASA elevation images.

Limitations: the terrain is procedural by default, physics values are estimates, and weather is a scenario rather than a live forecast.
details:
What it does and how it works
MarsPath is a browser-based 3D planning tool for astronaut surface walks on Mars. Users pick a start and a destination on a 12×12 km terrain model of Gale Crater or Jezero Crater, either from named landmarks such as Bradbury Landing and Yellowknife Bay or by clicking the map. An A* pathfinder computes three routes: safest, fastest and science-oriented. Each route is analyzed for distance, walking time (slowed by slope and loose sand), oxygen and battery use, radiation dose, and radio line of sight to the base, which is checked by ray-casting from the base antenna. The app applies a one-third oxygen rule (outbound, return and reserve), recommends a route with reasons, and suggests an EVA start hour from a 24-hour dust-storm scenario. A live walk simulation shows telemetry and a companion astronaut.

Benefits
MarsPath makes risk trade-offs visible before a walk begins. It turns hazards into measurable consumables and links each hazard to a route choice. It runs in any modern browser with no installation and works on phones. It uses NASA datasets as references, including Mars Trek, USGS, HiRISE, MOLA, and Curiosity and Perseverance mission data. Users can load a real NASA elevation image in place of the procedural terrain.

Intended impact
The tool is meant to support mission planners and crews in preparing surface walks, and to help scientists choose sampling routes that stay within safety margins. It can also teach students how planetary terrain, consumables and communications interact. Real elevation data for other sites can be loaded to extend it beyond the two sectors.

Tools and technologies
The app is written in HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. Three.js (r128) with OrbitControls renders the 3D terrain through WebGL, and the 2D elevation profile uses the HTML Canvas API. The core algorithms are custom: procedural terrain from fractal value noise, a binary-heap A* pathfinder, and ray-marched line-of-sight. Typography uses Google Fonts. Source control and hosting use Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages. Development was assisted by Claude, an AI assistant. No special hardware is required; any device with WebGL is enough.

What makes it creative
MarsPath treats oxygen and battery budgets as route constraints, not just distance. It shows three routing philosophies on one map for direct comparison. A dust-storm scenario changes speed, energy and oxygen use, not only the visuals. The companion astronaut and telemetry panel give the tool a mission-operations feel.

Factors the team considered
We considered crew safety (falls, sinking, extreme cold, radiation), consumables (oxygen and battery reserves), communication continuity, and science value (clay and sulfate units). We also considered usability for planners, with a clear status verdict and a responsive layout. We labeled data clearly as NASA source material or model estimate, and we state the limits of each.
